request.user:
[2020 summer phd math-stat — problem 2]

Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be a random sample from a multivariate $N_q(\mu, \Sigma)$ distribution. Consider the model $\mu = \eta a$ and $\Sigma = \alpha I + \beta a a'$, where $a \in \mathbb{R}^q$ is a fixed vector with $a'a = 1$, and $\eta, \alpha, \beta$ are unknown real parameters.
(a) Find necessary and sufficient conditions on $(\alpha, \beta)$ for $\Sigma > 0$ (positive definite).
(b) Find the eigenvalues of $\Sigma$, their corresponding eigenspaces and eigenprojections, and the trace of the eigenprojections.
(c) Find the MLE $\hat\theta = (\hat\eta, \hat\alpha, \hat\beta)$ of $\theta = (\eta, \alpha, \beta)$. Clearly justify why it is the MLE.
(d) Find the limiting distribution of $\sqrt{n}(\hat\alpha + \hat\beta - \alpha - \beta)$.
(e) Find $\mathbb{E}(\hat\theta)$. Use this to find minimum variance unbiased estimators of $\eta$, of $\alpha$ and of $\beta$. Clearly justify your answers.

response.text:
Let  
\[
A=aa',\qquad P=I-aa',\qquad \gamma=\alpha+\beta .
\]
Here \(A\) is the orthogonal projection onto \(\operatorname{span}(a)\), and \(P\) is the orthogonal projection onto \(a^\perp\). Also
\[
\Sigma=\alpha I+\beta aa'=(\alpha+\beta)A+\alpha P=\gamma A+\alpha P.
\]

For parts (c)–(e), assume \(q\ge 2\) and \(n\ge 2\). If \(q=1\), only \(\gamma=\alpha+\beta\) is identifiable, so \(\alpha,\beta\) cannot be estimated separately.

---

## (a) Positive definiteness

For any \(x\in \mathbb R^q\), write
\[
x=ta+z,\qquad z\perp a.
\]
Then
\[
x'\Sigma x
= \gamma t^2+\alpha \|z\|^2.
\]
Therefore, for \(q\ge 2\),
\[
\Sigma>0
\iff \alpha>0\quad\text{and}\quad \gamma=\alpha+\beta>0.
\]

Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{\alpha>0,\qquad \beta>-\alpha.}
\]

If \(q=1\), the \(a^\perp\) component is absent, and the condition is only \(\alpha+\beta>0\).

---

## (b) Eigenvalues, eigenspaces, eigenprojections

Since
\[
\Sigma=\gamma A+\alpha P,
\]
we have
\[
\Sigma a=\gamma a,
\]
and for every \(z\in a^\perp\),
\[
\Sigma z=\alpha z.
\]

Thus, when \(\beta\neq 0\), so that \(\gamma\neq \alpha\), the distinct eigenvalues are:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
\text{Eigenvalue} & \text{Eigenspace} & \text{Eigenprojection} & \text{Trace} \\
\hline
\gamma=\alpha+\beta & \operatorname{span}(a) & A=aa' & 1 \\
\alpha & a^\perp & P=I-aa' & q-1
\end{array}
\]

If \(\beta=0\), then \(\Sigma=\alpha I\), so the only eigenvalue is \(\alpha\), with eigenspace \(\mathbb R^q\), eigenprojection \(I\), and trace \(q\). The projections \(A\) and \(P\) are still reducing projections, but they are not distinct spectral projections in that degenerate case.

---

## (c) MLE of \(\theta=(\eta,\alpha,\beta)\)

Let
\[
Y_i=a'X_i,\qquad \bar Y=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i=a'\bar X.
\]
Also define
\[
S_Y=\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i-\bar Y)^2
\]
and
\[
T_\perp=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i'PX_i
=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i'(I-aa')X_i.
\]

Because
\[
\Sigma^{-1}=\gamma^{-1}A+\alpha^{-1}P
\]
and
\[
|\Sigma|=\gamma \alpha^{q-1},
\]
the log-likelihood, up to an additive constant, is
\[
\ell(\eta,\alpha,\gamma)
=
-\frac n2\log \gamma
-\frac{n(q-1)}2\log \alpha
-\frac{1}{2\gamma}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i-\eta)^2
-\frac{1}{2\alpha}T_\perp.
\]

The likelihood separates in \(\eta,\gamma,\alpha\).

For fixed \(\gamma\), the term \(\sum (Y_i-\eta)^2\) is minimized at
\[
\hat\eta=\bar Y=a'\bar X.
\]

Then maximizing in \(\gamma>0\) gives
\[
\hat\gamma=\frac{S_Y}{n}.
\]

Maximizing in \(\alpha>0\) gives
\[
\hat\alpha=\frac{T_\perp}{n(q-1)}.
\]

Since \(\gamma=\alpha+\beta\), the MLE of \(\beta\) is
\[
\hat\beta=\hat\gamma-\hat\alpha
=
\frac{S_Y}{n}
-
\frac{T_\perp}{n(q-1)}.
\]

Therefore,
\[
\boxed{
\hat\eta=a'\bar X,
\qquad
\hat\alpha=\frac{1}{n(q-1)}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i'(I-aa')X_i,
}
\]
and
\[
\boxed{
\hat\beta=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n (a'X_i-a'\bar X)^2
-
\frac{1}{n(q-1)}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i'(I-aa')X_i.
}
\]

These are the global maximizers because each separated likelihood term has a unique interior maximizer whenever \(S_Y>0\) and \(T_\perp>0\), which occurs with probability one under the model for \(n\ge2\), \(q\ge2\).

---

## (d) Limiting distribution of \(\sqrt n(\hat\alpha+\hat\beta-\alpha-\beta)\)

Since
\[
\hat\alpha+\hat\beta=\hat\gamma=\frac{S_Y}{n},
\]
and
\[
Y_i=a'X_i\sim N(\eta,\gamma),
\]
we have the exact distribution
\[
\frac{S_Y}{\gamma}\sim \chi^2_{n-1}.
\]

Therefore
\[
\sqrt n(\hat\alpha+\hat\beta-\alpha-\beta)
=
\sqrt n(\hat\gamma-\gamma)
=
\gamma\frac{\chi^2_{n-1}-n}{\sqrt n}.
\]

Since
\[
\frac{\chi^2_{n-1}-(n-1)}{\sqrt{2(n-1)}}\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}N(0,1),
\]
we get
\[
\boxed{
\sqrt n(\hat\alpha+\hat\beta-\alpha-\beta)
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
N\left(0,\,2(\alpha+\beta)^2\right).
}
\]

---

## (e) Expectations and MVUEs

We use the facts
\[
\frac{S_Y}{\gamma}\sim \chi^2_{n-1},
\qquad
\frac{T_\perp}{\alpha}\sim \chi^2_{n(q-1)}.
\]

Thus
\[
\mathbb E(\hat\eta)=\eta,
\]
\[
\mathbb E(\hat\alpha)
=
\frac{1}{n(q-1)}\mathbb E(T_\perp)
=
\alpha,
\]
and
\[
\mathbb E(\hat\gamma)
=
\mathbb E(\hat\alpha+\hat\beta)
=
\frac{n-1}{n}\gamma.
\]

Therefore
\[
\mathbb E(\hat\beta)
=
\frac{n-1}{n}(\alpha+\beta)-\alpha
=
\beta-\frac{\alpha+\beta}{n}.
\]

Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb E(\hat\theta)
=
\left(
\eta,\,
\alpha,\,
\beta-\frac{\alpha+\beta}{n}
\right).
}
\]

Now define
\[
T_1=\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i,\qquad
T_2=\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i^2,\qquad
T_3=T_\perp.
\]
The joint density can be written as a full natural exponential family:
\[
f_\theta
=
h(x)\exp\left\{
\frac{\eta}{\gamma}T_1
-\frac{1}{2\gamma}T_2
-\frac{1}{2\alpha}T_3
-A(\theta)
\right\},
\]
with natural parameter space
\[
\mathbb R\times (-\infty,0)\times(-\infty,0),
\]
which is open. Hence, by the completeness theorem for full-rank exponential families, \((T_1,T_2,T_3)\) is complete sufficient. Therefore, by the Lehmann–Scheffé theorem, any unbiased function of \((T_1,T_2,T_3)\) is the unique MVUE.

We already have unbiased estimators
\[
\hat\eta=a'\bar X
\]
and
\[
\hat\alpha=\frac{T_\perp}{n(q-1)}.
\]

For \(\beta\), use the unbiased estimator of \(\gamma=\alpha+\beta\):
\[
\frac{S_Y}{n-1}.
\]
Thus an unbiased estimator of \(\beta=\gamma-\alpha\) is
\[
\frac{S_Y}{n-1}-\frac{T_\perp}{n(q-1)}.
\]

Therefore the MVUEs are

\[
\boxed{
\delta_\eta=a'\bar X,
}
\]

\[
\boxed{
\delta_\alpha=
\frac{1}{n(q-1)}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i'(I-aa')X_i,
}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
\delta_\beta=
\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (a'X_i-a'\bar X)^2
-
\frac{1}{n(q-1)}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i'(I-aa')X_i.
}
\]

Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{
\delta_\beta
=
\frac{n}{n-1}(\hat\alpha+\hat\beta)-\hat\alpha
=
\frac{n}{n-1}\hat\beta+\frac{1}{n-1}\hat\alpha.
}
\]
